page.title: React Interview Questions for Freshers
page.description: The React questions asked of freshers and junior developers, with short answers you can say out loud: JSX, virtual DOM, props and state, hooks basics and keys.

intro.text: A fresher interview is a check for foundations, not for depth. Nobody expects you to have tuned a render loop. They expect you to know what React is doing when you call a state setter, and to notice when a question has a trap in it.

Almost every question below appears in almost every junior React interview. Work through them until you can answer each in two sentences without preparing, then follow a link when you want the reasoning behind one.

expect.text: What a fresher interview usually looks like

items: **A short screening call.** Definitions and vocabulary: what React is, JSX, components, props and state.
**A technical round of 45 to 60 minutes.** The same ground in more depth, plus hooks and lists, and usually one small coding task such as a counter or a to-do list.
**A code walkthrough.** You are shown a component with a bug, often a missing key, a mutated state array or a missing dependency, and asked what is wrong.
**Questions about your own project.** Expect "why did you do it that way" for something you built. Have one honest answer ready about a thing you would now do differently.

expect.title: The three that decide most fresher interviews
expect.text: Why keys matter and why the array index is a bad key. Why a state setter does not update the variable immediately. Why an effect with a missing dependency causes a stale value. If those three are solid, you are ahead of most candidates at this level.

items: **Days 1 and 2.** [React basics](/react-interview-questions/basics) and [components and props](/react-interview-questions/components-and-props). Build one small component from scratch each day, without a tutorial open.
**Days 3 and 4.** [Hooks](/react-interview-questions/hooks), concentrating on `useState`, `useEffect` and the rules of hooks.
**Day 5.** [Forms and events](/react-interview-questions/forms-and-events), then build a login form with validation.
**Day 6.** [Two or three coding challenges](/react-interview-questions/coding-challenges) under a timer, out loud, as if someone were watching.
**Day 7.** Re-read only the one line answers here, then take the [React quizzes](/quizzes) to find what has not stuck.

questions.question: What is React?
questions.shortAnswer: React is an open source JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of components, where you describe what the UI should look like for a given state and React works out how to update the DOM.

questions.question: What are the main features of React?
questions.shortAnswer: Component based architecture, declarative rendering through JSX, a virtual DOM with reconciliation, one way data flow, and the ability to render on the client, the server or to native platforms.

questions.question: What is JSX and why does React use it?
questions.shortAnswer: JSX is a syntax extension that lets you write markup inside JavaScript. It is not part of the browser: a compiler such as Babel or SWC turns it into ordinary function calls that create React elements.

questions.question: What is the virtual DOM and how does it work?
questions.shortAnswer: The virtual DOM is an in-memory tree of plain JavaScript objects describing the UI. On each render React builds a new tree, compares it with the previous one, and applies only the differences to the real DOM.

questions.question: What is the difference between the virtual DOM and the shadow DOM?
questions.shortAnswer: They are unrelated. The virtual DOM is a React implementation detail for computing updates in memory; the shadow DOM is a browser standard for encapsulating a component's DOM and styles from the rest of the page.

questions.question: What is the difference between a React element and a React component?
questions.shortAnswer: A component is a function or class that describes UI; an element is the plain object that component returns, describing one instance of what should appear on screen.

questions.question: What is the difference between props and state?
questions.shortAnswer: Props are data passed into a component from its parent and are read only inside that component. State is data a component owns and can change, and changing it triggers a re-render.

questions.question: What does unidirectional data flow mean in React?
questions.shortAnswer: Data moves in one direction only, from parent down to child through props. A child communicates back up by calling a function the parent passed it, rather than by writing to the parent's data.

questions.question: What are keys in React and why are they needed?
questions.shortAnswer: A key is a stable identifier that tells React which item in a list is which between renders, so it can move, keep or remove the right DOM nodes and component state instead of guessing by position.

questions.question: What is the difference between a class component and a function component?
questions.shortAnswer: A class component extends React.Component, holds state in this.state and uses lifecycle methods. A function component is a plain function that uses hooks for state and effects. Function components are the modern default.

questions.question: What are fragments and when would you use one?
questions.shortAnswer: A fragment lets a component return several children without adding an extra DOM node. Write it as <>...</> or <React.Fragment>...</React.Fragment>.

questions.question: What are React hooks and why were they introduced?
questions.shortAnswer: Hooks are functions that let a function component use state, effects and other React features. They were introduced in React 16.8 to make stateful logic reusable without wrapper components, and to stop related code being split across lifecycle methods.

questions.question: What are the rules of hooks, and why do they exist?
questions.shortAnswer: Only call hooks at the top level of a component or another hook, never inside conditions, loops or nested functions, and only call them from React function components or custom hooks. React identifies hooks by call order, so the order must be identical on every render.

questions.question: How does useState work?
questions.shortAnswer: useState returns a pair: the current value for this render and a setter. Calling the setter schedules a re-render with the new value; it does not change the variable you are currently holding.

questions.question: What is useEffect and when does it run?
questions.shortAnswer: useEffect runs a function after React has committed the render to the DOM and the browser has painted. It runs after every render by default, or only when a value in the dependency array has changed.

questions.question: What does the dependency array do, and what changes between no array, an empty array and a populated one?
questions.shortAnswer: No array means the effect runs after every render. An empty array means it runs once after mount. A populated array means it re-runs whenever one of those values changes by reference or value.

questions.question: What is useContext, and what are its limitations?
questions.shortAnswer: useContext reads the nearest provider's value for a context, letting a deep component get data without prop drilling. Its limitation is that every consumer re-renders whenever the provider's value changes, whatever part of the value they actually use.

questions.question: What is the children prop?
questions.shortAnswer: children is the special prop that holds whatever was written between a component's opening and closing tags. It is what makes wrapper components such as layouts, cards and modals possible.

questions.question: How do you give a prop a default value in a function component?
questions.shortAnswer: Use a JavaScript default in the destructuring: function Button({ variant = 'primary' }). The legacy Component.defaultProps object still works for classes but is deprecated for function components.

questions.question: What are the ways to do conditional rendering in React?
questions.shortAnswer: An if statement before the return, a ternary inside JSX, logical AND for the render-or-nothing case, or returning null to render nothing at all.

questions.question: How do you render a list, and what should you watch out for?
questions.shortAnswer: Map the array to elements and give each one a stable key. Watch for index keys, for mutating the source array, and for doing filtering or sorting work on every render.

questions.question: How do you validate props — PropTypes or TypeScript?
questions.shortAnswer: TypeScript, for anything new. It checks at compile time across the whole codebase, while PropTypes only warns in the console at runtime in development, and PropTypes was removed from React in version 19.

questions.question: What is a controlled component?
questions.shortAnswer: An input whose displayed value comes from React state and whose changes are written back to that state through an onChange handler. React is the single source of truth for the field.

questions.question: What is an uncontrolled component, and when would you prefer one?
questions.shortAnswer: An input that keeps its own value in the DOM, which you read with a ref or from the form data on submit. Prefer it for large forms where per-keystroke re-renders hurt, for file inputs, and when integrating with non-React code.

questions.question: How do you handle several inputs with a single change handler?
questions.shortAnswer: Give each input a name attribute and use it as the key when updating a state object: setValues((previous) => ({ ...previous, [event.target.name]: event.target.value })).

questions.question: How do you pass an argument to an event handler?
questions.shortAnswer: Wrap the call in an arrow function, or bind the value with a data attribute and read it from the event. Do not call the function directly in JSX — onClick={remove(id)} runs it during render.

questions.question: What are the phases of a React component's lifecycle?
questions.shortAnswer: Mounting, when the component is added to the DOM; updating, when props or state change; and unmounting, when it is removed. React also has an error phase for components that catch errors from their children.

questions.question: What are the main lifecycle methods in a class component?
questions.shortAnswer: constructor, render and componentDidMount for mounting; shouldComponentUpdate, render and componentDidUpdate for updating; componentWillUnmount for unmounting; plus getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch for errors.

questions.question: Why must state be treated as immutable in React and Redux?
questions.shortAnswer: Both detect change by comparing references. If you mutate an object in place, the reference is unchanged, so React skips the re-render and Redux's reducers and selectors see no change.

questions.question: What is lifting state up, and what is state colocation?
questions.shortAnswer: Lifting state up means moving a value to the closest common ancestor of the components that need it. Colocation is the opposite instinct: keep state as close as possible to where it is used, and only lift when something forces you to.

questions.question: What is React Router and why does React need a routing library?
questions.shortAnswer: React renders components; it has no concept of a URL. React Router maps URLs to components and keeps the address bar, history and back button in sync while the page is never actually reloaded.

questions.question: What is the difference between BrowserRouter and HashRouter?
questions.shortAnswer: BrowserRouter uses clean URLs through the History API and needs the server to serve the app for every path. HashRouter puts the route after a #, which the server never sees, so it works on any static host with no configuration.

questions.question: What is the difference between Link and a plain anchor tag?
questions.shortAnswer: An anchor triggers a full page load, throwing away the app's state and re-downloading everything. Link renders an anchor but intercepts the click and navigates through the router instead.

questions.question: How do you read route parameters and query strings?
questions.shortAnswer: useParams returns the dynamic segments of the matched path, and useSearchParams gives you a URLSearchParams object plus a setter for the query string.

questions.question: What is the difference between code splitting and lazy loading?
questions.shortAnswer: Code splitting is a build time concern: the bundler produces several chunks. Lazy loading is the runtime behaviour: a chunk or an asset is requested only when it is needed. Code splitting makes lazy loading of code possible.

questions.question: How do you type a component's props?
questions.shortAnswer: Declare a type or interface for the props object and annotate the destructured parameter. That is all React needs — the return type is inferred.

questions.question: How do you type children?
questions.shortAnswer: Use React.ReactNode, which covers elements, strings, numbers, arrays, null and undefined. Use React.ReactElement only when the child must be a single element.

questions.question: How do you type useState, and when is the type argument needed?
questions.shortAnswer: TypeScript infers the type from the initial value, so most calls need no annotation. You need the type argument when the initial value does not represent the full range, typically null or an empty array.

questions.question: Build a counter with increment, decrement and reset
questions.shortAnswer: One piece of state and three handlers. Use the functional updater form, and keep the initial value in a constant so reset has something to return to.

questions.question: Build a todo list with add, toggle and delete
questions.shortAnswer: One array of objects in state, updated immutably. Give each item a real id rather than using the index, and use a form so Enter submits.

questions.question: Build an accordion where only one section is open at a time
questions.shortAnswer: Hold the id of the open section in state rather than a boolean per section, so exclusivity is structural. Toggle to null when the open one is clicked again.

questions.question: Build a star rating component
questions.shortAnswer: Render a radio group styled as stars, track the committed value in state and the hovered value separately, and display the hovered value when there is one. Radios give you keyboard support for free.
